title: Can a planner beat selfish drivers?
hook: Every driver picks the faster road. Could a planner still make the average trip shorter?

knows: drivers pick the faster road (traffic equilibrium)
a road gets slower as more drivers use it
doesNotKnow: that the selfish equilibrium can be worse on average than a planner's split, by up to 4/3 with roads whose delay grows in proportion to traffic

misconception: If every driver picks the fastest route, the average trip is as short as it can be.
objective: The learner can explain that with road A at 60 min and road B at 60 min × its share, selfish drivers all take B and average 60 min, while a planner's half-and-half split averages 45 min, because each driver joining B slows everyone already on it; the ratio 4/3 is the worst case for delays proportional to traffic.

claims.text: With everyone on road B, the trip takes 60 minutes on both roads and no driver gains by switching; at any split with drivers on A, B is faster, so drivers on A want to switch.
claims.source: Road B delay = 60 × x for share x on B; road A = 60. For x < 1, 60x < 60, so a driver on A gains by moving; at x = 1 both are 60, so no one gains. claims.text: For roads whose delay is a fixed time plus a part proportional to traffic, selfish routing's total travel time is at most 4/3 of the best possible, and this two-road example reaches that bound.
claims.source: Roughgarden T. & Tardos É. (2002), 'How bad is selfish routing?', J. ACM 49(2): price of anarchy 4/3 for linear (affine) latency functions, attained by Pigou's two-link example (Pigou 1920, The Economics of Welfare). Easley & Kleinberg (2010), Networks, Crowds, and Markets, ch. 8. Attribution for the fact-checker to confirm. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): DISPUTED (wording of the class). Roughgarden & Tardos ('How bad is selfish routing?', FOCS 2000 / J. ACM 2002) prove the 4/3 bound for linear (affine) latencies a*x + b; confirmed by web search snippet only, paper PDF blocked. But the sentence says 'delays that grow in proportion to traffic', and road A (constant 60) is not proportional; with purely proportional delays a*x, equilibrium equals optimum (marginal cost 2ax is proportional to delay), so the example would not be in the stated class. Fix (builder, reveal and claim): 'With delays that are a fixed time plus a part proportional to traffic, that is the worst it can ever be.' | CLAIM FIX 2026-10-14 (demo-builder, W-193): Was 'delays that grow in proportion to traffic'. Reveal and claim now name the affine class (fixed time plus a part proportional to traffic), per the fact-checker's fix. Needs an independent check. · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: Reveal wording now 'a fixed time plus a part proportional to traffic' (affine). Bound re-derived: Wardrop equilibrium f satisfies sum l(f)f <= sum l(f)f*; for l = ax + b, l(f)f* <= l(f*)f* + a f^2/4 <= l(f*)f* + l(f)f/4, so C(f) <= (4/3) C(f*). Example: 60/45 = 4/3, so it attains the bound. Roughgarden-Tardos not opened; not relied on. · v5 (2026-10-14, demo-builder, learner r8): sentence cut from the reveal ('With delays that are a fixed time plus a part proportional to traffic, that is the worst it can ever be'); told context, word budget (learner r8 named it). The example's own 4/3 stays as c6. Withdrawn, not learner-visible. | v6 (2026-10-14, demo-builder, W-564 learner r9): REINSTATED. Learner r9 found that without it the example's 4/3 reads as a general law. Reveal: 'Selfish routing costs 60 / 45 = 4/3 of the best, a third more: the worst case for roads with a fixed time plus a part proportional to traffic.' (the affine class, per FC pass 21's fix; FC pass 23's derivation C(f) <= 4/3 C(f*) for l = ax + b). Builder statement, not self-verified; needs an independent check. Final v6 reveal (QA path, 82 body words; reveal-fit counts 92 with the verdict line): 'Selfish drivers all take B: 60 min. Your Lowest seen reads 45 min at 50%, and the trace rises on both sides. 30 is out of reach: A takes 60. / The line under the chart is why: 5 more drivers on B save 135 min; the 50 already there lose 150, which nobody choosing feels. / Selfish routing costs 60 / 45 = 4/3 of the best, a third more: the worst case for roads with a fixed time plus a part proportional to traffic.' | FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED by my own derivation. The learner text names no paper. For latencies l(x) = ax + b (a, b >= 0), a Wardrop equilibrium f satisfies sum l(f)f <= sum l(f)f*, and a f f* <= a f*^2 + a f^2/4 (since a(f* - f/2)^2 >= 0). So C(f) <= C(f*) + C(f)/4, i.e. C(f) <= (4/3)C(f*), on any network. The bound is attained here: 60/45 = 4/3. Numerical check: 20,000 random affine parallel-link instances, worst ratio 1.3331. Roughgarden and Tardos 2002 not opened; the attribution is in the source field only.

recall.question: Drivers choose freely between a fixed-time road and a road that gets slower with traffic. Compared with the best possible split, what can happen to their average trip?
options: It can be longer: each driver ignores the delay they add for others
The same: free choice finds the best split
Shorter: drivers know their own trips best
recall.why: At the selfish equilibrium no single driver can gain by switching, but each one who crowds the variable road slows everyone on it. A planner who holds some drivers back on the fixed road lowers the average; with linear delays the selfish cost is at most 4/3 of the best.
